stories.headline: From declaration to deposit: how federal storm aid reaches a household, and where it can stall
stories.dek: Ten weeks after Rafael, many Coastal Bend households have registered for FEMA aid and are still waiting. Here is how the process works, step by step, and what officials say applicants can do now.
body: Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall, many households on the Coastal Bend have registered for federal disaster aid and are waiting to hear back. Others have not registered at all. Here is how the process has worked so far, and what officials say applicants can do this week.

Why registration came when it did. When the federal disaster declaration came Sept. 18, it paid for debris removal and emergency protective measures, not aid to families. Help for households had to wait on damage assessments, which dragged as teams worked around spill-zone limits and flooded streets. The state asked for Individual Assistance in October, FEMA approved it Nov. 10, and registration opened Nov. 13 to long lines at recovery centers.

After you register. FEMA reviews each application and may ask for more documents. Renters, for example, may be asked to show they lived at the damaged address. "If we ask you for something, answer as fast as you can, and call the helpline if a letter doesn't make sense," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "A pending application is usually waiting on something. Find out what it is."

Getting paid. Approved aid is paid by check or by direct deposit. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and on Nov. 19 FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. The agency has urged every applicant to log in through its official website and verify where the money is set to go. It has not said how many accounts were affected.

Not registered yet? Phone and online registration count the same as standing in line, county officials say. "If two buses to a recovery center is what's stopping you, call instead, or find a church or neighborhood hub with a laptop out," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management.

Who is waiting longest. In the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, residents said help took days to arrive after the storm, and many households have no car. As the Ledger reported Monday, some applicants there now check their deposit details every morning while their applications sit.

Keep a folder. Put your registration number, every FEMA letter and a log of each call, with the date and the name of the person you spoke to, in one place. Ostrander said that record makes it faster to sort out a problem if one turns up.

stories.headline: Applied for FEMA aid? Check your deposit details before the holiday
stories.dek: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without permission. Here is how to check yours, and what to do if something looks wrong.
body: If you applied for FEMA disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael, take five minutes before Thanksgiving to check where your money is going.

FEMA confirmed Friday that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. That came two days after aid applicants in the Coastal Bend said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. The agency is urging every applicant to verify their deposit information now.

"Log in, look at your bank details, and if anything is off, call us right away," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Don't wait for a payment to go missing to find out."
Harborline 6's step-by-step guide from Saturday has the details. The five-minute version:
Open FEMA's site or app yourself, not from a link someone sent you, and sign in.
Find your payment details and hold them up against a check or your banking app.
See numbers you didn't enter? Call the FEMA helpline and your bank that day.
Last, swap your password for one you've never used anywhere else.
Ostrander said FEMA never charges a fee to apply and will never call to ask for your password. "If someone calls asking for it, hang up," she said. "That's not us."
No internet at home? A recovery center or a trusted neighbor can help you check. Don't share your password with anyone who helps you, and sign out when you're done.

Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and recovery centers have seen long lines since. Harborline 6 is following this story and will update it as FEMA releases more information.

stories.headline: FEMA: 410 aid accounts taken over in automated login attack; victims will be repaid
stories.dek: Attackers made about 220,000 login attempts using passwords stolen from other sites, FEMA says. The agency has added extra verification.
body: FEMA says 410 disaster-aid applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts, and applicants who were affected will be repaid.
The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen from other sites, according to the agency, and some of them worked. FEMA said Wednesday it has added extra verification to applicant accounts.

"If your account was one of them, you will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification, and we're asking everyone to check their deposit information today, even if you think you're fine."

The announcement comes a week after some Coastal Bend applicants reported that their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and five days after FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts. Harborline 6 reported Tuesday on how to check your deposit details.
FEMA did not say how much money was redirected or who was behind the login attempts. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
What changes for you:
The advice to confirm your bank details on FEMA's official website or app still stands.
If the password on your FEMA account is one you've used anywhere else, change it now. Start with your email account, because whoever controls your email can reset everything else.
Spot something off? FEMA and your bank both need to hear about it.
No internet access? The FEMA helpline or a recovery center can help you check your information.
Heading out of town for Thanksgiving? Do it before you go.
Harborline 6 will update this story as FEMA releases more information.

stories.headline: 410 accounts, 220,000 tries: FEMA details how aid accounts were hijacked
stories.dek: The agency says attackers used passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. A threat researcher says the method is common, cheap and aimed at reused passwords.
body: Attackers made about 220,000 automated attempts to sign in to FEMA disaster-aid accounts and took over 410 of them, the agency said Wednesday, putting numbers to a problem Coastal Bend applicants first reported last week.

The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen elsewhere, according to FEMA. The agency said it has added extra verification to applicant accounts and that applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.

"Every applicant affected will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification. Check your deposit information anyway, even if you're sure nothing changed."
FEMA did not say how much money was diverted, how many of the 410 accounts belonged to Coastal Bend residents or who was behind the attempts. Ostrander declined to discuss who might be responsible.

The sequence, according to FEMA and applicants: Individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. On Nov. 17, some applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. On Nov. 19, FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts and urged applicants to verify their deposit information. On Wednesday, the agency released the totals.

Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, said the figures fit a familiar pattern known as credential stuffing, in which attackers test stolen username and password pairs against a new site until some of them work.

"Fewer than two in every thousand attempts worked, and that's typical," Feld said. "It's a numbers game. Attackers get lists of leaked passwords, run them through software and wait for the people who reused one."
Feld said she would not guess who was behind the attempts. "That's for investigators to say, not me," she said.

The defense, she said, is unglamorous: a different password for every account, and a second sign-in step wherever one is offered. "Start with your email," Feld said. "If someone controls your email, they can reset everything else."
Applicants who see deposit details they don't recognize should contact FEMA and their bank, Ostrander said.

stories.headline: How "credential stuffing" got into hurricane aid accounts in Texas
stories.dek: FEMA says 410 disaster-aid accounts were taken over with passwords stolen from other sites. A researcher explains why the attack is cheap, automated and aimed at people who reuse passwords.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael struck the Texas coast, some people waiting on federal disaster aid have run into a second problem: someone else got into their accounts first.

FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts that used passwords stolen elsewhere. The agency said it has added extra verification and that affected applicants will be repaid. It did not say who was responsible or how much money was diverted.

Security researchers call the technique credential stuffing. Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab, described it in three steps. Attackers collect username and password pairs exposed in old data breaches at unrelated companies. They load those pairs into software that tries them, one after another, against a new target. Then they keep the ones that work.

"It's less breaking in than walking through doors people left unlocked somewhere else," Feld said. "If your password for a shopping site leaked three years ago and you use the same one for your aid account, that's the open door."

The math favors the attacker, she said. About 410 successes out of roughly 220,000 attempts is a success rate of about two-tenths of 1 percent, but each attempt costs almost nothing. Once inside, an intruder can change where a payment is deposited.

That is what applicants on the Coastal Bend began reporting Nov. 17, when some said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access two days later.

Disaster aid draws this kind of attack because payments are urgent and applicants are stretched, Feld said. "People are living in damaged houses, borrowing phones, logging in wherever they can," she said. "They're not thinking about password hygiene, and nobody should blame them for that."

The best defenses, she said, are a unique password for each account, a password manager and a second sign-in step such as a code sent by text or an app. "FEMA adding verification helps," Feld said. "But the long-term fix is people not reusing passwords, and that's a habit, not a patch."
Asked who might be behind the attempts, Feld declined to speculate. "That's for the government to say," she said.

stories.headline: A season to be thankful for: station and depot families mark Thanksgiving after Rafael
stories.dek: From the September evacuation to a fall of relief flights and repairs, it has been a long autumn for the NAS Corpus Christi and Army depot community.
body: Ten weeks ago, the flight line at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi sat empty. Training aircraft from the station and from NAS Kingsville had flown to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Corpus Christi Army Depot had halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.

This Thanksgiving, there is plenty to be grateful for. Training aircraft began coming home six days after landfall. The depot, which took hangar roof damage and water intrusion in the storm, is back at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. And in October, the station hosted 26 military C-17 relief flights and 14 civilian charters that carried supplies into a region that had spent weeks under a boil-water notice.

"This community packed up, came back and went straight to work helping everybody else," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "That's what we're thankful for. Enjoy the time with your families this week. You've earned it."

The depot workforce has its own reasons for gratitude. "Our people came back to hangars with water on the floor and holes in the roof, and they got the mission running again," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them did that while they were fixing their own homes at night."

It has not been an easy fall. The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption in October; power was restored and the cause remains under review. The Fort Hood aviation brigade scheduled to move through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer was delayed by the storm and again by the October channel closure before its equipment began loading onto a sealift ship Nov. 12.

For families still dealing with storm damage at home, FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. If you applied, check your deposit details, and use a password you don't use anywhere else.
From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: a safe and restful Thanksgiving to every sailor, soldier, civilian and family member who carried this community through the fall.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving in the fellowship hall: a relief hub feeds a neighborhood still waiting
stories.dek: Ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church hub served a holiday meal to neighbors waiting on aid, repairs and answers.
body: By 10 a.m. Thursday, the line outside the fellowship hall reached the church sign and bent around the corner. Inside, volunteers in plastic gloves carved turkeys on folding tables, and a teenager with a clipboard asked every family the same question: "How many at home?"

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, 59, has run a relief hub from this hall since the first days after Hurricane Rafael, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay. On Thanksgiving, the hub did what it has done all fall, only with gravy.
"People think the storm is over because the boil-water notice is over and the news moved on," Whitfield said. "Come stand at my door. The storm is over for some people. It's not over here."

The streets around the church are part of the low-lying, low-income stretch near the bay where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Many households here have no car, a gap advocates warned about over the summer, when they pushed for more evacuation rides. In late October, health officials said emergency room visits across the region were back near normal, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

FEMA opened individual assistance registration Nov. 13. Whitfield said volunteers have spent much of the past two weeks helping neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, since FEMA's warning about unauthorized account access, check whether anyone has changed their deposit details. On Wednesday, the agency disclosed that attackers armed with passwords stolen from other sites had taken over 410 applicant accounts. It said affected applicants would be repaid.
"Half my people don't have an email address, and the other half share one with a cousin," Whitfield said. "And now we're telling them to watch out for hackers. Lord, have mercy."

By late morning the hall had run out of rolls, and a volunteer drove to the grocery store for more. Children ate pie on the steps. An older man in a Navy veteran's cap asked if he could take a plate to a neighbor who couldn't walk that far, and a volunteer made up two.
Whitfield said the hub would stay open through the holidays.
"We'll be here at Christmas, too," she said. "I'm not going anywhere, and neither are they."

stories.headline: On Black Friday, a gutted Port Aransas bait shop sells from coolers and waits for winter
stories.dek: Ten weeks after Rafael's landfall, Coastal Bend small businesses head into the holiday season with damaged storefronts, closed bays and customers stretched thin.
body: Bill Hargrove's Black Friday sale is written in grease pencil on a sheet of plywood: "LIVE SHRIMP. CHEAP ADVICE. NO REFUNDS ON EITHER."

Hargrove, 64, has sold bait and tackle near the Port Aransas jetties for years. Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm made landfall on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Ten weeks later, he is selling out of coolers on the porch while a carpenter works inside.
"Black Friday on the island used to mean the Winter Texans rolling in and buying a rod they didn't need," Hargrove said. "This year it's me, two coolers and whoever's brave enough to drive out."

Rafael hit at the end of a strong summer. Port Aransas businesses reported busy bait shops and charters in August. Then the storm pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties.

For businesses that depend on the water, the fall brought one closure after another. The ship channel closed Sept. 13 ahead of the storm and only partly reopened Oct. 14. An explosion near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28 closed it again for 14 days, until Nov. 11. And because of the oil spill, fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have stayed closed since Sept. 18.
The reopened channel matters for the port, where crude exports resumed in mid-November. For a bait shop, Hargrove said, it matters less than people think.
"Big ships don't buy bait," he said. "Fishermen buy bait. And the bays are closed."
Back in Corpus Christi, shoppers lined up before dawn outside big-box stores on South Padre Island Drive. Plenty of carts held more plywood, box fans and extension cords than televisions.
Hargrove said he hopes to have the shop's walls closed in by Christmas, depending on the drywall crew.
"They're on island time, too," he said. "I can't complain. I invented island time."

stories.headline: Bays stay closed as the fall season slips away for Coastal Bend fishers
stories.dek: More than two months after the oil spill, fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Fishers are filing damage claims and waiting.
body: The nets on Huy Nguyen's shrimp boat are dry, folded and stacked, and the boat is tied up at Aransas Pass the way it has been most of the fall.
"Ten weeks, and I fished zero days in the bay," said Nguyen, 51, a second-generation shrimper. "My father used to say a boat that doesn't move is just an expensive house for pelicans."

Nguyen's boat survived Hurricane Rafael. His season did not. As the storm arrived in mid-September, surge and wind carried crude oil from two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal out of the ship channel and into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The Unified Command estimated the release at about 9,000 barrels, and sheen spread across about 33 square miles of water, marsh and shoreline.

Fishing in both bays has been closed by Texas Parks and Wildlife since Sept. 18, when the Texas Department of State Health Services also stopped shellfish harvesting; the fishing closure was extended in early October. It remains in place as the fall bay season winds down, and the oyster season that opened Nov. 1 has brought no harvest from the closed waters.

Shoreline cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28. Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said the health and wildlife agencies will keep the closures until the science supports lifting them.
"Nobody wants these bays open more than the people who fish them," Whitaker said. "And nobody wants them open too early, either."

The claims center run for the tankers' owners began taking lost-income claims from fishers and shoreline businesses Nov. 16. Nguyen filed his claim two days later, bringing a grocery bag of fuel receipts and the eleven spiral notebooks his father taught him to keep.
"I write everything down. Pounds, price, fuel, ice," he said. "They want numbers, I have numbers. What I don't have is a paycheck."

Whitaker said fishers should keep records of lost trips and expenses and file with the owners' claims center. Bay shrimpers had reported a fair start to the season in July, Nguyen said, though fuel costs were already squeezing margins before the storm took the rest.
Asked about Thanksgiving, Nguyen shrugged.
"We ate. Family came. Nobody asked me about the boat," he said. "That was the gift."

stories.headline: Navy suspends air station's emergency fuel supplier pending quality review
stories.dek: The review of Quellmar Fuel Partners is linked to the October failure of a backup generator at NAS Corpus Christi, the station says. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
body: The Navy has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that has supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi since Hurricane Rafael, pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October, the station said Sunday.

"We have suspended the supplier while a fuel quality review is completed," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We take the reliability of the station's power seriously, and we're not going to get ahead of the review."

Quellmar disputed the move. "All product we delivered meets specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager. "We'll cooperate with the Navy's review, and we expect it to confirm that."

Federal contract records that became public in early October show the Navy awarded Quellmar a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the air station after the station's regular supplier flooded in the storm.

On Oct. 25, the station said its backup generator had failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the station said at the time that the cause was under review. Sunday's announcement was the first time the Navy publicly tied that review to the station's fuel.

Hale declined to say how long the review would take, what it had examined so far or how the station is being supplied while it is under way, saying the station does not discuss details that bear on security.
Kerr said the company had answered the call when the station needed fuel. "We stepped up when the regular supplier was under water, and we'd do it again," she said.

Naval Air Station Corpus Christi trains Navy pilots and hosts Corpus Christi Army Depot, the Army's main helicopter repair depot. The station's training aircraft flew to Fort Worth ahead of the storm and began returning six days after landfall.

stories.headline: Fact check: No, the county's debris contract isn't $140 million, and FEMA hasn't stopped paying families
stories.dek: A new wave of posts claims contractors are "stealing aid." Some questions about emergency contracts are fair. These specific claims are false.
body: A new wave of viral posts claims contractors are stealing hurricane aid from Coastal Bend families. Harborline 6 checked the most-shared claims. Some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. These specific posts are false.

CLAIM: The county handed a debris company $140 million. FALSE. The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC on Sept. 24, according to public records. The $140 million figure appears in posts with no source.

CLAIM: FEMA stopped paying families so the money could go to contractors. FALSE. FEMA individual assistance registration remains open in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Aid to households and county cleanup contracts are paid through separate programs.

One widely shared post from @CoastTruthTX, an account that spread false claims after landfall that the military was seizing homes, reads: "THEY GOT RICH OFF OUR STORM. Contractors are STEALING your aid and nobody will say it." The post offers no evidence.

WHAT'S FAIR TO ASK: The debris contract was awarded without competitive bidding, and news organizations including the Bayside Ledger have requested records on emergency contracts. Separately, the Navy said Sunday it has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Those questions have answers still to come.

"Ask us about any contract. The records are public, and you'll get an answer," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "What I'm asking is, check before you share. A made-up number doesn't hold anybody accountable."
Before you share: look for a source document, check the date and be wary of all-caps posts that say nobody else will report something.

stories.headline: Giving Tuesday: how to make sure your storm donation reaches Coastal Bend neighbors
stories.dek: Relief groups say needs remain ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael. A freight manager who moved relief cargo explains why cash goes further, and how to give safely.
body: Tomorrow is Giving Tuesday. On the Coastal Bend, the need hasn't gone anywhere.

Church and neighborhood hubs have handed out food and water since the first days after Hurricane Rafael, sometimes before official distribution reached their streets. Many are still running ten weeks later.

Terry Akins knows what it takes to move donated goods. His company, Gulf Relief Logistics, handled 40 relief containers that waited out the anchorage backlog for weeks before the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider finally berthed in October, about a month late.

"Stuff is heavy. Money moves at the speed of light," said Akins, the company's regional manager. "A pallet of water somebody collected three states away is a lot of diesel and a lot of forklift time before it gets here. Give money to people who are already here."
Before you give:
Give to groups you know, like a local church, food bank or school.
Type the web address yourself. Don't tap a link in a text or social media post.
Be wary of anyone who wants payment by gift card, wire transfer or cryptocurrency.
Watch out for lookalike sites that copy the names of real charities or agencies.
Ask what your money will buy. A good local group can tell you.

If you applied for FEMA aid yourself, check your own account, too. Last week FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were hijacked with passwords stolen from other sites. Affected applicants will be repaid, the agency says. FEMA never charges a fee to apply.
"The stuff that helps most right now is boring," Akins said. "Diapers, cleaning supplies, grocery cards. Nobody takes a picture of a grocery card. It still feeds a family."

stories.headline: Fuel supplier disputes Navy suspension as review of air station generator failure continues
stories.dek: Quellmar Fuel Partners says every delivery met specifications. The Navy says it won't get ahead of a quality review tied to October's generator failure at NAS Corpus Christi.
body: On an ordinary day, a backup generator is the least interesting machine on a military installation. It sits, it gets tested, and it waits for the moment the grid goes down. At Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, that moment came in October, and the generator failed.

Now the Navy has suspended the company that supplied the station's emergency fuel after Hurricane Rafael. The station said Sunday that Quellmar Fuel Partners was suspended pending a fuel quality review linked to the generator failure. On Monday, the company pushed back.

"Every load we delivered met specifications, and we have the paperwork to show it," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager. "We stepped in when the station's regular supplier was flooded out. We're disappointed, and we're cooperating with the review."

Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station, said the review would run its course. "The review will determine what happened," he said. "Until it's complete, we're not going to speculate about the cause."

Some background helps explain what is at stake. Military fuel is bought to written specifications, and suppliers typically provide paperwork certifying that a delivery meets them. A quality review generally checks those records, and any samples kept, against what the contract requires. The Navy has not said what its review has examined or what, if anything, it has found.

The timeline, from public statements and records: The station's regular fuel supplier flooded in the storm. Federal contract records that became public Oct. 4 showed a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station to Quellmar. On Oct. 25, the station said its backup generator had failed during a power interruption, that power had been restored and that the cause was under review. On Sunday, the Navy tied that review to fuel quality and suspended the supplier.
For people who live and work on the station, Hale said, the power is on. He declined to discuss backup arrangements, citing security.
Kerr said she expects the company to be cleared. "When the facts come out, they'll show we did our job," she said.
The Navy has not said how long the review will take.

stories.headline: Why the new rumor wave about "stolen aid" spreads, and how to sort real questions from false claims
stories.dek: Posts claiming contractors are stealing hurricane aid mix legitimate questions with invented details. A threat researcher explains why that mix travels fast in neighborhoods still waiting for help.
body: The posts land between photos of curbside debris piles and requests for a working dryer. Contractors are stealing your aid, they say, and nobody will tell you.

It is the second big rumor wave since Hurricane Rafael. In the first days after landfall, viral posts falsely claimed the military was seizing homes and that aid would go only to wealthy neighborhoods. This one, which picked up over the Thanksgiving weekend, is about contracts.

Fact-checkers say some of the questions are legitimate and some of the specific posts are false. The county's $14.2 million emergency debris contract went to Vantorra Restoration without competitive bidding, a fair subject for scrutiny. On Sunday, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier, Quellmar Fuel Partners, pending a fuel quality review; the company says its fuel meets specifications. But posts claiming the debris contract was worth $140 million, or that FEMA stopped paying families to pay contractors, are false, Harborline 6 found.
Dana Feld, a threat researcher at Northlight Threat Lab who studies influence campaigns, said the mix is the point.

"The most effective false stories are built around something true," Feld said. "A real contract, a real delay, real anger. Then somebody adds a number that isn't real, and the true part carries the false part along with it."

The posts land hardest where people are still waiting. Residents in low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and many are still waiting on aid applications filed since registration opened Nov. 13.
"When people are waiting, any story that explains the wait feels true," Feld said. "That's not a character flaw. That's being human in a bad month."

Feld offered a short checklist. Find the document behind the claim. Check any number against public records. Notice when a post leans on all-caps outrage instead of evidence. And ask whether the post wants you to click, donate or share before you've had time to think.
Asked who is behind the new posts, Feld declined to say. "I don't do attribution by vibes," she said.
Questions about a specific contract can go to the agency that awarded it. County contract records can be requested from the county, and federal contract awards are posted in public databases.

stories.headline: Hurricane season ends today. On the Coastal Bend, Rafael's season doesn't.
stories.dek: The Atlantic season officially closes Nov. 30 after forecasters called for an active year. For the bays, the water plant and the people who live by them, recovery keeps its own calendar.
body: The Atlantic hurricane season officially ends today, and nobody on the Coastal Bend is throwing a party.

In late August, forecasters expected above-normal activity for the rest of the season. Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Sept. 4, crossed the Yucatan, became a hurricane in the southern Gulf four days later and made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm.

"The calendar says the season's over, and the odds of another storm here this late are very low," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "But the end of the season isn't the end of the storm for anybody still fixing a roof."

Rafael's footprint is still visible. A surge of about 11 feet swept into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays, and floodwater covered about 43 square miles of the three coastal counties. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds, and a citywide boil-water notice lasted from Sept. 18 to Oct. 23. About 9,000 barrels of crude escaped two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal, and the surge spread sheen across about 33 square miles of bay and shoreline.

Dr. Nathan Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, said the timing made the spill worse. "For a few hours, the surge moved the whole bay inland," he said. "Whatever was floating in the ship channel moved with it."

Cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, but fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Brooks cautioned against expecting a quick timeline. "Marshes recover on the scale of seasons and years, not weeks," he said. "The honest answer is that we'll know more after another season of monitoring."

Arceneaux said the off-season is the time to prepare for the next one. Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and he said that advice stands.
"Check your insurance, write down your plan, and if you don't have a ride out, tell somebody now, not when the cone is over your house," he said. "June comes faster than you think."

stories.headline: Season-end log: Corpus Christi channel lost weeks to Rafael, spill restrictions and the jetty blast
stories.dek: The ship channel closed Sept. 13, partly reopened Oct. 14 and closed again for 14 days after the Oct. 28 explosion at the entrance. It has been open since Nov. 11.
body: The Atlantic hurricane season ends today with the Corpus Christi Ship Channel open, after a fall in which the port lost weeks of normal operations to Hurricane Rafael, an Inner Harbor oil spill and an explosion at the entrance channel.
Sept. 11: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Rafael. The port stays open; terminals wind down crude loading.
Sept. 12: Port Condition Yankee closes the port to inbound traffic. Fourteen vessels hold at the offshore anchorage. Crude exports halt.
Sept. 13: Port Condition Zulu closes the channel to all traffic; anchorage ships put to sea. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval.
Sept. 14 to 15: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas. Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth.
Sept. 17: Ships return from sea to the anchorage. The channel stays closed for surveys.

Oct. 14: Channel partly reopens. Inner channel stays restricted for spill decontamination. Anchorage backlog delays relief cargo; MV Gulf Provider berths Oct. 17 with 40 relief containers, about a month late.

Oct. 28: Around 1 a.m., an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties damages the tug and injures two crew. Coast Guard closes the channel. Separately, spill-related inner channel restrictions are lifted as cleanup moves to monitoring.
Oct. 30: Navy says an explosive device caused the blast; a joint Navy-Coast Guard search of the channel is under way.
Nov. 5: Navy teams find a second device near the entrance channel and render it safe.
Nov. 11: Channel reopens after a 14-day closure and full sweep. Exports resume. The next day, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment begins loading onto a sealift ship.

"The channel is open, and we intend to keep it that way," said Javier Salinas, spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The people who work this port had a hard fall. They've earned a quiet winter."

Open items: Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems; the maintenance vendor Brightwake Marine Systems has said its remote credentials were misused. The FBI is investigating the blast.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the service does not comment on open investigations. "Our focus is safe navigation, and the channel is open," she said.

stories.headline: Column: Ask hard questions about storm contracts. Don't pass along fake numbers.
stories.dek: The new rumor wave about "stolen aid" borrows real questions and buries them under false claims. Coastal Bend residents deserve real answers.
body: I have covered two hurricanes before Rafael, and each one brought a second storm: the one that blows through our phones.

This week's version says contractors are "stealing aid." Posts claim the county's debris contract is worth $140 million. Public records show it is $14.2 million. Posts claim FEMA stopped paying families so it could pay contractors. FEMA registration remains open. Those claims are false, and Harborline 6's fact-checkers said so Sunday.
Here is what bothers me most: the false posts make it harder to ask the true questions.

The county awarded its debris contract to Vantorra Restoration sole-source, without competitive bidding, ten days after landfall. That is allowed in an emergency. It also deserves a close look after the emergency. On Sunday, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier, Quellmar Fuel Partners, pending a fuel quality review tied to October's generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Those are fair questions, and they deserve documented answers.

My colleagues on the Ledger's investigations desk file records requests on every emergency contract. It is slow work. It does not go viral. It is how you learn whether what was billed matches what was done.

Some of the loudest posts come from accounts that spread false claims after landfall that the military was seizing homes. @CoastTruthTX, one of the most shared, is back at it. An account that was wrong about your house in September does not get the benefit of the doubt about your aid in November.

So here is my ask. Before you share, look for a document. If a post has a number, check it. If it has no number, ask why. If you have a real question about a contract, send it to the county or the Navy, or send it to us.

Families in the low-income neighborhoods near the bay waited days for help after this storm. Many are still waiting on aid applications and repairs. They deserve accountability built on records, not on somebody's all-caps guess.
Marisol Treviño covers city government and disasters for the Ledger.

stories.headline: Debris contractor billed for 2.3 times the debris county surveys estimated, records show
stories.dek: Invoices and survey estimates obtained by the Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for far more debris than the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling.
body: Vantorra Restoration LLC, the company awarded a $14.2 million sole-source contract to clear Hurricane Rafael debris, billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated, according to records obtained by the Bayside Ledger.

The Ledger obtained the company's invoices and the county's survey estimates through public records requests filed after the contract was awarded Sept. 24. Taken together, the records show the tonnage Vantorra billed running at roughly 2.3 times the tonnage the county's surveys estimated.
Vantorra denies overbilling.

"We bill for what we haul, load by load, and every load is documented," said Derek Sloane, the company's managing partner. "Our crews have been working around the clock since this storm hit. Pictures from the sky don't pick up debris. Trucks do."

Survey estimates are not exact counts, and the records alone do not show why the figures differ. Drone and satellite surveys estimate how much debris is on the ground; invoices reflect what a contractor says it hauled. The records do not show which figure is closer to what was actually removed.

The county awarded the contract without competitive bidding in the storm's second week, as debris blocked streets across the region. Emergency rules allow sole-source awards when delays would endanger the public, and such contracts typically draw scrutiny once the emergency passes.

Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county had received the Ledger's questions. "We're looking at the records, and I'm not going to get ahead of that," he said.

The Ledger shared its findings with Vantorra before publication. Sloane said anyone who doubts the company's numbers is welcome to see the work for themselves. "Ride along with one of my trucks," he said. "Bring a lunch."
The Ledger has requested additional records on the contract, including payments to date. Those requests are pending.

stories.headline: Debris contractor denies overbilling after report finds billed tonnage at 2.3 times county estimates
stories.dek: Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. The company says it bills for what it hauls.
body: The company hired to haul away Hurricane Rafael's debris is pushing back today after a newspaper investigation raised questions about its bills.

Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million emergency debris contract that the county awarded without competitive bidding in September, as debris blocked streets across the region.

Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane denies overbilling. "I've got trucks, I've got drivers, and I've got a ticket for every load," Sloane told Harborline 6 by phone. "We've been working around the clock for these folks since the water went down. Come count 'em with me."
The records do not show why the two figures differ. Survey estimates are not exact counts, and invoices reflect what a contractor says it hauled.
Emergency rules allow contracts to be awarded without bidding when delays would endanger the public, but those contracts usually get a closer look once the emergency passes.

County emergency management spokesman Dwayne Pruitt said the county is reviewing the records and would not comment further today. The Ledger said it shared its findings with Vantorra before publishing.
What this means for you: The county has not announced any change to debris pickup. If debris is still sitting at your curb, contact the county with pickup questions.
What's next: The Ledger says it has requested more records on the contract, including payments to date. Harborline 6 will follow the county's response and update this story.

stories.headline: Load tickets and flyovers: how storm debris is counted, and why Vantorra's bills are drawing questions
stories.dek: The Ledger found Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage county surveys estimated. Here is how debris is generally measured, and what the company says.
body: Every truckload of storm debris is supposed to leave a paper trail.

After a disaster, debris haulers are generally paid by the amount they remove, measured by volume or by weight. Trucks are measured before they start. Each load is supposed to get a ticket recording what was hauled, from where and to which disposal site. Monitors often check loads along the way.

Aerial surveys work from the other direction. Drones and satellites photograph debris on the ground, and analysts estimate how much is there before anyone picks it up. Neither method is perfect. Surveys can miss debris hidden under roofs or trees. Tickets can be wrong if a truck's capacity is overstated or a load is counted twice.

That is why the gap the Ledger reported Wednesday matters. Records obtained through public records requests show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated under the $14.2 million sole-source contract the county awarded Sept. 24. Which number better reflects what was actually hauled away, the records do not say.
In an interview Wednesday, Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, denied overbilling and said the surveys, not the invoices, are the problem.

"Surveys are guesses. Tickets are facts," Sloane said. "A picture from a few hundred feet up can't see what's under a pile of wet drywall and a fallen oak. My guys can, because they're the ones lifting it."

Sloane said the company's load records are on file with the county. "We've been working around the clock since the water went down," he said. "I'm proud of these crews, and I'll put my tickets up against a satellite any day."
Asked why the gap was so large, Sloane said he had not seen how the county's surveys were done and would not comment on them. "I'm not a satellite guy," he said. "I'm a trucks guy."
The county has not announced any change to the contract. The Ledger has asked the county for the load tickets and monitoring records that support the invoices and will report what they show.

stories.headline: Fuel supplier suspension: what station families need to know
stories.dek: The Navy has suspended NAS Corpus Christi's emergency fuel supplier pending a quality review tied to October's generator failure. Here are answers to families' most common questions.
body: Families have been asking about Sunday's news that the Navy suspended the station's emergency fuel supplier. Here is what we know from the station's public affairs office and public records.

What happened? The Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar has supplied emergency fuel under a $2.1 million contract awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael.

Is the power on? Yes. Power was restored after the October interruption. "The station has power, and keeping it that way is a priority," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. Hale said he would not discuss backup arrangements in detail.
What does the company say? Quellmar says its fuel met specifications, and operations manager Nadia Kerr has said the company will cooperate with the Navy's review.
How long will the review take? The Navy hasn't said. "I don't have a timeline to give you," Hale said. "When there's something we can release, we'll release it."
Do families need to do anything? No. Hale said there is no action for families to take.
Where should I get updates? From official station channels and the Anchor & Rotor. If you see a claim about the station online, check it against an official source before you share it.

Also this week: If your family is still repairing storm damage, FEMA individual assistance registration remains open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. FEMA urges every applicant to check their deposit details regularly, and to use a password they don't use anywhere else.
Holiday hours and family events will appear in next week's edition. The Anchor & Rotor will report on the fuel review when the Navy releases results.

stories.headline: Fact check: The debris billing report is real, but it doesn't show "stolen aid checks"
stories.dek: Viral posts are stretching a Bayside Ledger investigation into claims it doesn't support. Here is what the records show, and what they don't.
body: A real news report is being stretched into a false claim.

WHAT'S TRUE: The Bayside Ledger obtained records showing Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage estimated by the county's own drone and satellite surveys. The company denies overbilling. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract with the county.

CLAIM: "The debris company billed 2.3 times its contract." MISLEADING. The 2.3 figure compares tons billed with tons the surveys estimated. It does not compare dollars billed with the $14.2 million contract value, and the Ledger did not report how much the company has been paid.

CLAIM: "This proves contractors stole your FEMA check." NO EVIDENCE. The Ledger's report concerns billing for debris removal under a county contract. It says nothing about FEMA payments to individual households, and the posts offer no evidence for that claim.
One post from @CoastTruthTX reads: "SEE?? We TOLD you. They are stealing YOUR aid." The account previously spread false claims that the military was seizing homes after landfall.

Fact-checkers have said since the rumor wave began Nov. 28 that some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. The Ledger's records are exactly that kind of question. The posts built on top of them are not.
How to check a claim yourself: find the original report, read past the headline and compare any number in a post with the number in the source.

If you're worried about your own aid: Log in to your FEMA account through the official website or app and check your application status and deposit details. Questions about debris pickup go to the county.

stories.headline: County pauses payments to debris contractor Vantorra pending audit
stories.dek: The pause follows a Ledger report that the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. Vantorra denies overbilling and says it welcomes the audit.
body: The county has paused payments to Vantorra Restoration LLC, the company hired under a $14.2 million sole-source contract to clear Hurricane Rafael debris, pending an audit, a county spokesman said Friday.

"Until the audit is done, payments on that contract are on hold," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "That's not a finding of anything. It's us counting before we pay."

The pause comes two days after the Ledger reported that records obtained through public records requests show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage that the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The company has denied overbilling.

Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner, said the company welcomed the audit. "Our tickets will speak for themselves," he said. "In the meantime, I've got crews with families to take care of at Christmas, and I'm asking the county to move quickly."

Pruitt declined to say how much the county has paid Vantorra so far, who would conduct the audit or how long it would take. He said residents with questions about debris on their streets should continue to contact the county.

The county awarded the contract Sept. 24, ten days after landfall, without competitive bidding. Emergency rules allow sole-source awards when delays would endanger the public. The Ledger requested records on the contract soon after it was awarded and has since asked for the load tickets and monitoring records that support the company's invoices.

Debris removal has been one of the most visible parts of the recovery since Rafael made landfall Sept. 14. An audit is not a criminal proceeding, and the county has not accused the company of wrongdoing.

The Ledger's reporting found that the tonnage figures diverged; it did not determine why. Sloane has said the county's surveys, not his company's invoices, are the problem. "Surveys are guesses," he told the Ledger Wednesday. "Tickets are facts."

stories.headline: County halts payments to debris contractor while it audits the bills
stories.dek: The county says the pause on payments to Vantorra Restoration is "not a finding of anything." The company denies overbilling.
body: The county is putting payments to its hurricane debris contractor on hold.

County officials say payments to Vantorra Restoration are paused pending an audit. The move comes two days after the Bayside Ledger reported records showing Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated.

"We're not accusing anybody of anything today," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We're doing the math before we write the next check. That's what you'd do with your own money, and this is your money."

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, and debris lined streets across the region for weeks. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million emergency debris contract that the county awarded without competitive bidding ten days later. The company has denied overbilling, and its managing partner, Derek Sloane, has said the county's surveys undercount the debris his crews haul.
The records the Ledger obtained show the gap, not the reason for it. A survey estimate is not a count, and an invoice is the contractor's own tally of what it hauled.
How long will the audit take? The county hasn't said.
What it means for you: The county has not announced any change to debris pickup. Questions about debris on your street still go to the county.
Watch what you share: The pause is not a finding of wrongdoing, and no audit results have been released. Harborline 6 has already seen posts claiming otherwise.
Harborline 6 will update this story as the audit moves forward.

stories.headline: In Calallen, the tap water is safe again. Trust is taking longer.
stories.dek: Six weeks after the boil-water notice was lifted, some residents near the O.N. Stevens plant still reach for bottled water. Here is what the utility says, and what to do now.
body: Leticia Ramos keeps a case of bottled water by her back door, a habit she says she can't shake.

"My head knows it's fine. My hand still goes for the bottle," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who lives in Calallen, not far from the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant. This fall, she organized her neighbors' runs to water distribution sites.

The plant, the city's only water treatment plant, lost both of its power feeds early in Hurricane Rafael, and pumps were damaged. A citywide boil-water notice followed Sept. 18. Replacement pump parts were delayed when the supplier's local warehouse flooded and parts had to ship from out of state. They arrived Oct. 20, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23 after repairs and testing.

The weeks in between were hard on the city's health. Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal at their peak before easing in late September.

"The notice was lifted after repairs and testing, and the water meets standards," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "We know we asked a lot of people this fall, and we're sorry for that. We also understand it takes time to trust the tap again."
What you can do:
Water you stored in jugs during the fall can go to plants or cleaning. Refill with fresh tap water.
If you have a refrigerator water filter or ice maker and haven't already done so, replace the filter and throw out old ice, as is generally recommended after a boil-water notice.
If a faucet hasn't been used in weeks, run cold water for a few minutes before drinking from it.
If you have questions about your water, call the utility.
Ramos said she made her Thanksgiving turkey brine with tap water. "That's progress," she said. "Next step is the coffee."
She still wants more from the city. "What I want is for somebody to tell us what's being done so this doesn't happen again," she said. "Not a press release. A plan."
Gallegos said the utility would share more about its plans as they develop.

stories.headline: North Beach in December: quiet sand, pelicans and a neighbor who still checks the tide line
stories.dek: More than two months after oil washed ashore on North Beach, cleanup has moved to monitoring. Marcus Bell still walks the shoreline every morning, looking for black.
body: Marcus Bell walks North Beach at 7 a.m., hands in his jacket pockets, eyes on the tide line.
"I'm looking for black," said Bell, 67, a retired welder. "Haven't seen any in a while. Doesn't mean I quit looking."

Bell has had a front-row seat to Rafael. When the storm hit Sept. 14, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, cutting North Beach and Portland off from downtown until the bridges reopened after inspections Sept. 17. Then came the oil. Surge and wind carried crude out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and it washed onto North Beach and Portland shorelines and into marshes.
"I smelled it before I saw it," Bell said. "Like somebody left a truck running in your kitchen."

In September, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from people near oiled shorelines, and health officials told residents to avoid contact with oil. Those complaints were easing by early October, health officials said.

Shoreline cleanup moved into a monitoring phase Oct. 28. Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program, said that means the shoreline is still being watched and crews respond if anything turns up.
"Monitoring isn't walking away," Whitaker said. "If somebody sees oil, we want to know about it."

If you see oil or an oiled animal, don't touch it. Report wildlife to the hotline that opened in September, and report oil to the spill response. Fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.
On a gray December morning, the beach belongs mostly to Bell, a man flying a kite and a line of brown pelicans cruising the surf.
"Pelicans came back before the people did," Bell said. "Smartest residents we've got."
He spent Thanksgiving with neighbors, he said, frying a turkey in a driveway and arguing about the bridge. "Everybody's got a bridge story now," he said. "Mine's the best one, but I'm biased."

stories.headline: Five weeks after the jetty blast, a tug deckhand counts the days until he can go back out
stories.dek: Eddie Fontenot was one of two crew members hurt when an explosive device detonated beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay. He and his captain talk about recovery, routine and the channel they work.
body: Eddie Fontenot flexes the fingers of the arm that spent most of November in a cast. They work. He seems a little surprised.
"Arm's good. Head's mostly good," said Fontenot, 29, a deckhand for Laguna Towing. "I sleep with the TV on now. That's new."

Fontenot was one of two crew members injured around 1 a.m. Oct. 28, when an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties. He suffered a broken arm and a concussion. The blast damaged the tug, and the Coast Guard closed the ship channel.

Two days later, the Navy said the blast was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the channel with the Coast Guard, and on Nov. 5 they found a second device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe. The channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. The FBI is investigating.

Capt. Ray Dupree, 56, has towed ships in the Corpus Christi channel for 30 years and was master of Corrin Bay that night. He said he has been back on the water since mid-November, once the company had a boat for him.
"The channel's been swept end to end by people who know what they're doing," Dupree said. "I trust them. I run it every day. My crew runs it every day."
Dupree said he gets one question more than any other: who did it. He doesn't answer it.
"I drive tugs," he said. "The FBI can do their job, and I'll do mine."
Fontenot hopes to be cleared to go back to work after the new year. He said he misses the routine more than the paycheck, though he misses the paycheck, too.
"People think I'd be scared to go back out," he said. "I'm more scared of sitting on my couch until March."
Dupree said there is a spot on his crew whenever the doctor signs off. "He's a good hand," Dupree said. "He was a good hand that night, too. First thing he asked was whether everybody else was OK."
For now, Fontenot is spending the holidays with family and going to physical therapy. He has one goal for Christmas.
"Sleep through the night," he said. "With the TV off."

stories.headline: Damp walls and cold fronts: renters in storm-hit homes head into winter
stories.dek: In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, renters still waiting on repairs are bracing for colder nights. A health district epidemiologist offers advice for damp, drafty homes.
body: When the first real cold front of the season blew through Corpus Christi, Rosa Elizondo pulled every blanket in the duplex onto one bed and put her three children in it.
"The heater works. The window doesn't close all the way since the storm," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay. "So we have a heater that heats the street."

Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, Elizondo is still waiting on her landlord to fix the window and the water-stained ceiling, and on a FEMA application she filed the week registration opened Nov. 13. She is not alone. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and in late October, health officials said emergency room visits there were still about 40% above normal, even as the rest of the region had returned to near normal.

Renters face a particular bind. They can't make major repairs themselves, and many can't afford to move. In neighborhoods where many households have no car, even getting to a hardware store or a recovery center can take half a day by bus.
Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, offered general advice for damp, drafty homes.

"If you see or smell mold, clean small areas with soap and water and let in fresh air when you can," Shah said. "If anyone in the home has asthma or another breathing problem, call your doctor sooner rather than later. And please, never heat your home with a gas stove, an oven or a grill. Carbon monoxide doesn't smell like anything."

Shah said people with lingering health concerns after the storm should not wait for a crisis. "If you've been coughing for weeks or your child's asthma is getting worse, that's a reason to be seen," she said.
Elizondo said she has learned to improvise. She tapes plastic over the window at night and takes it down in the morning, so the landlord can see the damage if he ever comes by.
"Mis hijos think it's camping. Indoor camping," she said. "I let them think it. Camping is free."

stories.headline: Fact check: The county's pause on debris payments doesn't freeze FEMA aid, and no audit has found theft
stories.dek: Posts about the county's decision to pause payments to its debris contractor are spreading with two false claims attached.
body: Posts about the county's pause on payments to its debris contractor are spreading with two false claims attached. Here's what's true and what isn't.

WHAT'S TRUE: The county paused payments to Vantorra Restoration on Friday pending an audit. The pause followed a Bayside Ledger report that records show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra denies overbilling.

CLAIM: "Your FEMA money is frozen too." FALSE. The pause applies to payments under the county's debris contract. FEMA individual assistance to households is a separate federal program, and registration remains open in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
CLAIM: "The audit already proved they stole millions." FALSE. The audit has not been completed, and no findings have been released. The county has not accused the company of wrongdoing.
"There are no findings yet," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "When there are, you'll hear them from us, not from a meme."

This is the third set of claims Harborline 6 has checked since a wave of posts about contractors and aid began Nov. 28. Fact-checkers have found that some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. The specific posts checked here are not.
How to check a claim yourself: look for a source document, check the date and compare any number with public records.
Questions about your own FEMA application go to FEMA's helpline or official website. Questions about debris pickup still go to the county.

stories.headline: Federal inspector general opens review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend
stories.dek: The review adds federal scrutiny to storm contracts this fall, after the county paused payments to its debris contractor and, in a separate matter, the Navy suspended the air station's emergency fuel supplier.
body: A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend awarded after Hurricane Rafael, the Ledger confirmed Tuesday.

The Ledger could not immediately determine which specific contracts the review includes or how long it will take. Inspectors general are independent watchdog offices inside federal agencies that audit and investigate how federal money is spent.
Two emergency contracts in the region have drawn public scrutiny this fall.

On the debris side, the county awarded Vantorra Restoration LLC a $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract Sept. 24. Records obtained by the Ledger and reported Dec. 1 show Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The county paused payments to Vantorra on Friday pending an audit. The company denies overbilling.
"We've got nothing to hide," said Derek Sloane, Vantorra's managing partner. "Bring on the reviews. Every one of them is going to find the same trucks and the same tickets."

In a separate matter, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar held a $2.1 million emergency contract awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded. The company says its fuel meets specifications.
"We'll cooperate fully with any review," said Nadia Kerr, Quellmar's operations manager, who repeated that all product the company delivered met specifications.
Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management, said the county would cooperate with federal reviewers. "Whatever they ask for, they'll get," he said.
An inspector general's review is not a criminal charge or a finding of wrongdoing. Such reviews can end in public reports, recommendations to agencies or referrals for further action.
The Ledger has filed records requests on emergency contracts since the storm's first weeks and will continue to report on the review.

stories.headline: Federal watchdog to review Coastal Bend storm contracts
stories.dek: A federal inspector general is reviewing emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded after Hurricane Rafael. Here's the background, and what it means for you.
body: A federal watchdog is now looking at emergency contracts signed after Hurricane Rafael.

A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend, the Bayside Ledger reported Tuesday. It's not yet clear which contracts are included or how long the review will take. The review adds federal scrutiny to contracts signed in the first weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, when agencies moved fast to clear roads and restore services.
Here's the background:

Debris: The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract to Vantorra Restoration in September. Records obtained by the Ledger show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. The county paused payments Friday pending an audit. Vantorra denies overbilling, and its managing partner told the Ledger the company has nothing to hide.

Fuel: In a separate case, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review tied to the station's October generator failure. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications and that it will cooperate fully with any review.
What's an inspector general? An independent office inside a federal agency that audits and investigates how federal money is spent. A review is not a criminal charge and not a finding of wrongdoing.
What it means for you: Nothing changes for residents today. The county has not announced any change to debris pickup, and questions about debris on your street still go to the county.
Harborline 6 will follow the review and update this story.

stories.headline: What a federal inspector general review is, and what it isn't
stories.dek: A federal watchdog is reviewing emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend. Here is how such reviews generally work, and how this one differs from the county's audit and the Navy's fuel review.
body: A federal inspector general opened a review this week of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded in the Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael. Here are answers to readers' common questions.

What is an inspector general? Most federal departments and many agencies have one: an independent office that audits programs and investigates fraud, waste and abuse involving federal money. Inspectors general report to their agency's leadership and to Congress, and many of their findings are published.
What is being reviewed? Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend. The specific contracts and the timeline have not been announced.

Does a review mean someone did something wrong? No. A review is neither a charge nor a finding that anyone did wrong. Reviews can end with a report that finds no problems, with recommendations to agencies or with referrals for further action.

How is this different from the county's audit? The county paused payments to its debris contractor, Vantorra Restoration, on Friday pending its own audit, after records obtained by the Ledger showed the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. That audit is the county's. The company denies overbilling.

How is it different from the Navy's review? Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, was suspended by the Navy on Nov. 28 pending a review of fuel quality connected to the station's October generator failure. That review is the Navy's. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

Why would a federal watchdog look at these contracts? Emergency work after a federally declared disaster can be paid for or reimbursed with federal money, and federal agencies sign their own emergency contracts, as the Navy did for fuel. Either can bring a federal watchdog into the picture.
How long do these reviews take? It varies. Many take months, and some take more than a year.

Where can I see the records? Federal contract awards are posted in public databases, and county contracts can be requested under the Texas Public Information Act. The Ledger requests records on every emergency contract and reports what it finds.

stories.headline: Federal watchdog reviews hurricane contracts on Texas coast as recovery stretches into winter
stories.dek: An inspector general is examining emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded after Hurricane Rafael, adding federal scrutiny to a recovery marked by disputed contractor bills.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded on the Texas Coastal Bend after Hurricane Rafael, bringing federal scrutiny to a recovery already marked by disputes over storm contracts.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles. The storm knocked out power to Corpus Christi's only water treatment plant, leaving the city under a boil-water notice for five weeks, and disrupted a port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports by analysts' estimates.
In the weeks after landfall, agencies signed emergency contracts quickly, as they typically do after disasters. Two of those contracts have since drawn scrutiny.

The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC. Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger, a local newspaper, show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. The county paused payments last week pending an audit. The company denies overbilling.

Separately, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review linked to the failure of the station's backup generator in October. Quellmar, which received a $2.1 million emergency contract after the station's regular supplier flooded, says its fuel meets specifications.
"We'll cooperate with any federal review," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If they need documents from us, they'll have them."
It was not clear which contracts the review covers or how long it will take. An inspector general's review is not a criminal charge, and such reviews can end in reports, recommendations or referrals.

Emergency contracting after hurricanes has long drawn scrutiny nationally, because speed is the priority when roads are blocked and power is out, and the checks usually come afterward. On the Coastal Bend, residents are still rebuilding: federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the storm.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude heads into year-end after two fall shutdowns
stories.dek: Exports from the largest U.S. crude gateway resumed when the ship channel reopened Nov. 11. The bigger question for next year is confidence, not capacity, an analyst says.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi head into the final weeks of the year with the ship channel open, after a fall in which shipments halted twice: first when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic Sept. 12 ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and again after an Oct. 28 explosion at the Port Aransas jetties shut it for 14 days.

The port handles an outsized share of U.S. crude exports, about half by analysts' estimates. Before the storm it was loading tankers at near-record pace, and exports hit a monthly high at the end of August.

"Two closures in one quarter, from two completely different causes. That's what buyers will remember," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Exports resumed when the channel reopened. The question now is confidence, not capacity."

The first shutdown outlasted the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, but spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted until Oct. 28, and an anchorage backlog delayed cargoes; 14 vessels had queued offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic. The second halt came Oct. 28, the same day the inner-channel restrictions were lifted, when a blast beside a harbor tug closed the channel again. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device Nov. 5, and the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.
"The channel is open, and we're moving barrels," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi.
Holloway said the open investigation keeps some uncertainty in the market. The FBI is investigating the blast, and officials have not said who was responsible.
"Markets can price a hurricane. There's a century of data on hurricanes," she said. "An open question is harder to price."

stories.headline: Holiday season on the station: remembrance, rest and a reminder to check your accounts
stories.dek: As the bases mark Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day and head into the holidays, here is what station and depot families need to know this week.
body: Tuesday was Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day, and for a station community that spent the fall rebuilding, the call to remember those who served landed close to home this year.

"This community knows what it means to show up when things go wrong," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "This fall, our sailors, civilians and families did that over and over. We're proud of them heading into the holidays."

At Corpus Christi Army Depot, the workforce is closing out a year that included a hurricane, hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and a return to full production in late October with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

"Our people have earned some time with their families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them spent the fall fixing hangars by day and their own houses at night. We want them to rest."

FEMA accounts: If your family applied for FEMA aid for storm damage, check your account and confirm your deposit details. FEMA has added extra verification to applicant accounts. Use a password you don't use anywhere else, and never share it with anyone who calls or knocks.

Holiday decorating: If storm water got into your home's wiring or outlets this fall, have an electrician check them before you plug in holiday lights. Use outdoor-rated cords outside, and don't run cords under rugs or tarps.

Fuel supplier review: The Navy's fuel quality review involving Quellmar Fuel Partners, the station's suspended emergency fuel supplier, is ongoing. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Hale said the station would share results when it can. This week a federal inspector general also opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend; Hale referred questions about that review to the inspector general.
