Have a holiday event, a homecoming or a family milestone to share? Send it to the Anchor & Rotor, and we'll do our best to get it in before the new year.

stories.headline: Twelve-hour shifts and a season that won't quit: an ER nurse heads into the holidays after Rafael
stories.dek: Charge nurse Alyssa Cortez worked through the oil-spill complaints and the stomach-illness wave. Now she's bracing for flu season, and has advice for readers.
body: Alyssa Cortez can tell you which week of the fall was the worst by what her emergency department ran out of.

"First it was eye wash and inhalers for the folks near the oil. Then it was hallway beds for the stomach bug. Then it was everything, all at once," said Cortez, 34, a charge nurse at a Nueces County emergency department who works twelve-hour shifts.

The fall came in waves. Within days of landfall, emergency rooms saw respiratory and skin complaints from residents near oiled shorelines. After the boil-water notice, wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness rose to about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use, before easing in late September. By late October, visits were back near normal across most of the region, health officials said, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where they were still about 40% above normal.

Cortez said she can't discuss individual patients, but she notices patterns. "I still see the same neighborhoods more than I'd like," she said. "People who couldn't leave, couldn't get to a clinic, waited too long. They come to us because we're open."

Now she is bracing for the usual winter rush. Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District, said the habits that helped during the fall's stomach-illness wave apply to flu season, too.
"Wash your hands, stay home when you're sick, and get your flu shot if you haven't," Shah said. "It's not too late."
What readers should know:
For a cough, cold or minor injury, a primary care doctor or urgent care clinic is often faster than an emergency room.
Go to the emergency room or call 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke or a serious injury.
If you're caring for someone at home with a stomach bug, keep them drinking fluids and watch for signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or little urine.
Cortez is working Christmas Eve. She volunteered.
"Somebody's got to," she said. "Might as well be somebody who knows where the eye wash is."

stories.headline: Inner Harbor spill: shoreline in monitoring, remote-access probe still open
stories.dek: Nearly three months after about 9,000 barrels of crude escaped two tankers at the Rendal Terminals berth, investigators have not released findings on how the cargo systems were accessed.
body: Status of the Inner Harbor spill response and investigation as of Dec. 10:

Release: About 9,000 barrels of crude from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived in mid-September, according to the Unified Command of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Texas General Land Office. Surge and wind carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays; sheen covered about 33 square miles.

Response: Shoreline cleanup moved to a monitoring phase Oct. 28, when inner-channel restrictions for vessel decontamination were lifted. Nueces and Corpus Christi bays are still closed to fishing and shellfish harvesting. The claims center run for the tankers' owners, open since Sept. 26 for cleanup and property damage claims, began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.

Investigation: The Coast Guard disclosed Sept. 20 that investigators, assisted by federal cyber teams, were looking at possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. On Sept. 22, Brightwake Marine Systems, a vendor that maintains tanker cargo-control systems, said its remote-maintenance credentials had been misused and that it had revoked all remote access. No findings have been released.
"The investigation remains open, and we are not in a position to discuss it," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

Brightwake chief executive Owen Pryce said the company has not switched remote access back on. "We're rebuilding how remote access works here from the ground up, and nothing gets turned back on until we're certain," he said. "We owe that to the crews and to everyone who lives on that water."
Rendal Terminals said it continues to cooperate. "We are cooperating fully with the Unified Command and with investigators," said Victor Lang, a company spokesperson.

Kim Tran, a regional cybersecurity advisor with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has supported the investigation, offered general guidance for operators. "Any operator that lets a vendor connect remotely should know who is connecting, when and why, and should be able to shut that door fast," she said.
Gulfwater will report findings when they are released.

stories.headline: Christmas lights over blue tarps: a Calallen block decorates storm-damaged homes
stories.dek: Neighbors on Leticia Ramos's street are stringing lights on houses still waiting for roof repairs. Before you plug in, here's how to do it safely.
body: The tarps are still on. The lights are going up anyway.
On Leticia Ramos's block in Calallen, several houses still wear blue tarps from Hurricane Rafael. This week, neighbors started wrapping them in Christmas lights.

"We spent the fall hauling water jugs up and down this street," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who organized neighbors' water runs during the boil-water notice. "This December, we're hauling extension cords. It's a contest now. I'm losing."

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant near Calallen lost both power feeds early in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice before it was lifted Oct. 23. Some roofs on the block are still waiting on repairs.

Ramos's students made paper snowflakes for her front window. A neighbor set a light-up pelican on top of a tarp. Another strung lights along a fence still leaning from the wind. The lights come on at dusk, and kids from nearby streets have started walking over to see them.
"It's not about pretending it didn't happen," Ramos said. "It's about saying we're still here."
Before you plug in:
If storm water reached your outlets, wiring or breaker box, have an electrician check them first.
Use lights and extension cords rated for outdoor use.
Don't staple or nail lights through a tarp. That's how water gets in.
Don't overload outlets, and turn the lights off when you go to bed.
Keep cords out of puddles and away from downspouts.
Harborline 6 wants to see your lights. Send your photos through the Harborline 6 app.

stories.headline: Geminid meteor shower peaks Monday night: a Flour Bluff skywatcher's tips
stories.dek: Jaime Ortega, whose videos of lights over the air station drew attention in September, says this week's show is the real thing, and easy to explain.
body: Jaime Ortega has his folding chair, his thermos and his tripod ready for Monday night.

The Geminid meteor shower, one of the best of the year, peaks Monday night into early Tuesday. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see dozens of meteors an hour, though this year a full moon will wash out the fainter ones.
"This one's easy. It's little bits of rock burning up," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer in Flour Bluff. "No mystery. Just get away from the streetlights and give your eyes twenty minutes."

Ortega knows something about mysterious lights. In September, he posted videos of lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi at night. At the time, the station said it knew of the drone reports and was working with authorities; the FBI confirmed an investigation. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.
"I haven't filmed anything like that since," Ortega said. "I still look. Most of what people send me now is planes, satellites and Venus. That's fine. Keep sending it."
Tips for watching:
Start after 10 p.m. The show usually gets better after midnight.
Get away from city lights. A dark beach or a rural road works, but follow posted hours and don't park on the shoulder.
Lie back and look at a wide patch of sky. You don't need a telescope or binoculars.
Dress warm. The breeze off the bay gets cold after dark in December.
Put your phone away. The screen ruins your night vision.

Ortega plans to film the shower and post the best streaks. "If anybody sees something that isn't a meteor, tell me," he said. "I'll tell you what it probably is. I'm careful with the word 'probably.'"
Check the Harborline 6 forecast before you head out. Clouds could get in the way.

stories.headline: On a feast day, a toy table: families near the bay make room for the holidays
stories.dek: As parishes marked the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Sunday, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's relief hub opened a toy table for families still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.
body: Before dawn Sunday, las mañanitas drifted from a parish down the street, where families gathered with roses for the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe. By 9 a.m., a different line had formed outside Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall.

Inside, donated toys sat sorted by age on the same folding tables that held turkeys at Thanksgiving and water jugs in September. Parents picked one gift for each child and wrapped it at a table in the back, where volunteers had paper, tape and strong opinions about bows.

"Nobody's kid should have to learn about hurricanes and Santa Claus in the same year and decide Santa's the one who isn't real," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from the hall since the first days after the storm.

Rosa Elizondo came with a list for her three children and left with two of the three items checked off. "Este año, Santa viene en autobús," she said: This year, Santa comes by bus. Elizondo doesn't have a car. Neither do many of her neighbors, a gap advocates raised long before the storm.

Nearly three months after Hurricane Rafael, the hall remains a lifeline for the low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13, and volunteers here have helped neighbors without smartphones fill out applications and, after FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were taken over using stolen passwords, check their deposit details.
Elizondo said her application is still pending. "I check the bank every morning. Every morning it's the same," she said. "Same is good. Same means nobody took it."

Among the volunteers carrying boxes in from a pickup were a few young sailors from the air station, there on their own time and in civilian clothes. One of them spent twenty minutes helping a grandmother choose between two dolls.
Volunteers also kept a table of donated coats and blankets by the door, a reminder that many families near the bay are still living in homes with storm damage as the nights get colder.
Whitfield said she is already thinking past Christmas.
"December, everybody remembers you," she said. "January is when the donations stop and the bills come. Remember us in January."

stories.headline: Half their share: low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got less storm aid and waited longer for 911, analysis finds
stories.dek: An analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher finds low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
body: In the days after Hurricane Rafael came ashore, the 911 center serving Corpus Christi and Nueces County took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, nearly ten times normal, and most came from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Three months later, an analysis shows how those neighborhoods fared once help started moving.

Low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, according to an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. The median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

"Half. Not a little less. Half," Marquez said. "These are the neighborhoods with the fewest cars, the least flexible jobs and often the least reliable internet. When getting help depends on getting somewhere or getting online, this is the pattern you'd expect, and it's the pattern we found."

The analysis compared groups of census tracts: the lowest-income tracts inside the surge or flood zone, where many households have no vehicle, and the highest-income tracts in Nueces County. It measured each group's share of aid dollars against its share of residents and compared typical 911 response times.

The findings put numbers on what residents and advocates described all year. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps left many households without cars in neighborhoods near the bay. When the order to leave came, those without cars depended on county buses and waited for them. After landfall, residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets. In late October, emergency room visits there were still about 40% above normal while the rest of the region was back near normal.

"We told anybody who would listen," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now it's got a number on it. I hope the number does what my voice couldn't."
Marquez cautioned that the analysis shows where the gap is, not every reason for it. "This tells you who got less, not why in every case," she said. "That's the next question, and it's answerable."
Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

stories.headline: How we measured the aid gap: a guide to Coastline's analysis with Texas A&M-Corpus Christi
stories.dek: What "half their share" means, why the analysis uses medians for 911 response times, and what the numbers can and can't tell you.
body: Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. Here is how to read those numbers.

Which neighborhoods were compared? The analysis compared two groups of census tracts. The first is the lowest-income tracts inside the storm surge or flood zone, which also have some of the highest shares of households without a vehicle. The second is the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

What does "half their share" mean? If aid dollars were distributed in proportion to population, each group would receive a share of aid equal to its share of residents. The low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received about half of that.

Why measure by residents and not by damage? "Per resident is the simplest fairness test. It isn't the only one," Marquez said. "Comparing aid to damage is worth doing too, and we'd welcome anyone who wants to try it with us."

What is a median 911 response time? The median is the middle value: half of responses were faster, half slower. Medians aren't thrown off by a handful of extreme cases. A median 2.1 times as long means the typical call in those neighborhoods waited a little more than twice as long for a response as the typical call in high-income areas.

What can't the analysis tell you? It shows where the gap is, not every cause. "Factors worth examining include road and bridge closures during and after the storm, vehicle access, internet access and how people learned about aid," Marquez said. After the storm, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway stayed closed until inspections were finished Sept. 17, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown.
Does it say anyone acted wrongly? No. It measures outcomes. Explaining them, and deciding what to change, comes next.
What data was used? Census demographics, 911 response records and aid payment totals, each analyzed by census tract.
Have a question we didn't answer? Send it to the Coastline newsroom, and we'll add answers to this guide.

stories.headline: Low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of storm aid, analysis finds
stories.dek: The analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher also found the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "I could have told them that for free," one resident said.
body: Rosa Elizondo read the number off her phone Monday morning and laughed, not happily.
"Half? I could have told them that for free," said Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who rents near the bay and has no car.

In Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, low-income neighborhoods got aid dollars at about half their share of residents, an analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, found. The analysis also found that the median 911 response time in those neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
"About half" is how the researchers summarized the ratio. The Ledger has not independently analyzed the underlying data.

Marquez said the result reflects who could reach help. "When getting help depends on a car, a smartphone or a day off work, the people without those things fall behind," she said. "The storm didn't treat everyone the same, and neither did the recovery."

The findings match what the Ledger has heard from residents since September. Residents without cars spent the evacuation waiting on county buses. After the storm, the 911 center took about 2,900 calls a day at the peak, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay, and residents of low-income neighborhoods reported waiting days for help. Church hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Elizondo applied for FEMA individual assistance the week registration opened Nov. 13, riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending, she said, and the ceiling in her rental still bears water stains from the storm.
"Everybody keeps telling me to be patient," she said. "I am patient. I'm the most patient woman in Texas. Patience doesn't fix a roof."
Marquez said the next step is understanding the causes. "The number tells you where to look," she said. "Now somebody has to go look."

stories.headline: Poorer neighborhoods hit by Hurricane Rafael got about half their share of aid, analysis finds
stories.dek: An analysis of storm aid and 911 response on the Texas coast found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents and waited longer for emergency help.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — Low-income neighborhoods in the path of Hurricane Rafael's storm surge received disaster aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas, according to an analysis released Monday.

The analysis, by Coastline Public Radio, a regional public radio newsroom, and Dr. Sofia Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi, compared the lowest-income census tracts inside the surge or flood zone with the highest-income tracts in Nueces County.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 hurricane, with about 11 feet of surge in Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Calls to the region's 911 center peaked at about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, most from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay.

"Disasters don't create inequality. They reveal it, and then they compound it," Marquez said. "The households with the fewest resources were the most exposed to the surge and the least able to get to help afterward."

Researchers who study disasters have documented similar gaps after other storms, Marquez said, but local numbers matter because they point to local fixes. She said aid agencies could close part of the gap by bringing registration into neighborhoods rather than waiting for residents to come to them.

Federal individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties opened Nov. 13. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay reported waiting days for help after the storm, and local churches and neighborhood groups filled gaps before official distribution arrived.
The analysis did not determine the causes of the gap. Marquez said factors worth examining include vehicle access, internet access and road and bridge closures in the days after landfall.

The region is still recovering. Corpus Christi spent five weeks under a boil-water notice after the storm knocked out power to its only water treatment plant, and fishing remains closed in two bays affected by an oil spill during the hurricane.

stories.headline: Three months after Rafael: where the Coastal Bend stands
stories.dek: The water is safe, the channel is open and the bays are still closed. Aid, contracts and investigations remain unfinished business.
body: Three months ago today, Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. as a Category 3 storm, pushing about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooding about 43 square miles across three counties. Here is where the recovery stands.

Water: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both power feeds in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice. Replacement pump parts arrived Oct. 20 after delays, and the notice was lifted Oct. 23.

Aid: Residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties have been able to register for FEMA individual assistance since Nov. 13. FEMA said Nov. 24 that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere; it added verification and said affected applicants will be repaid. On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income surge-zone neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

The bays: Shoreline cleanup from the roughly 9,000-barrel spill moved to monitoring Oct. 28, but fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The tanker owners' claims center began taking lost-income claims Nov. 16.
"I'm a fisherman who doesn't fish," said Huy Nguyen, 51, an Aransas Pass shrimper who filed his claim in November. "Ask me in the spring."

The port: The ship channel reopened Nov. 11 after a 14-day closure that followed the Oct. 28 explosion near the jetties, and exports resumed. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment began loading the next day. The FBI is investigating the blast. Investigators are also still examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill.

Contracts: The county paused payments to debris contractor Vantorra Restoration on Dec. 3 pending an audit, after records obtained by the Ledger showed the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated; the company denies overbilling. Separately, on Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, which had supplied emergency fuel to the air station, pending a fuel quality review. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications. A federal inspector general followed on Dec. 7 with a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the region.

On the island: Bill Hargrove, 64, is still rebuilding his bait shop near the Port Aransas jetties. "Three months? Feels like three years," he said. "But the drywall's half up, and the pelicans don't care what month it is."

stories.headline: "We told them in September": neighbors react to analysis showing an aid gap
stories.dek: A church relief hub leader and a North Beach resident say the finding that low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of aid matches what they lived through.
body: Pastor Gloria Whitfield doesn't need a spreadsheet to know who got help after Hurricane Rafael. She has a sign-in sheet.

"We told them in September. We told them in October," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now there's a study, and everybody's surprised. I'm not surprised. I'm tired."

An analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. In those neighborhoods, the median 911 response time ran 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
Whitfield's hub handed out food and water in the first days after the storm, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay.
On North Beach, Marcus Bell, 67, remembers the days when the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway were closed and his neighborhood was cut off from downtown.
"When the bridges closed, you were on your own. Nobody was getting to us fast," said Bell, a retired welder. "I had neighbors who never even tried to call."
The analysis didn't determine the causes of the gap, and the researcher behind it says that's the next question.
What you can do:
If you haven't registered for FEMA individual assistance, registration is still open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.
If you don't have a phone or internet, church and neighborhood hubs have been helping neighbors apply.
If you already applied and have questions about your status, FEMA's helpline can help.
Harborline 6 will keep following the response to the findings.

stories.headline: Researcher behind the aid-gap analysis lays out fixes: knock on doors, follow the bus lines
stories.dek: Dr. Sofia Marquez says the gap in Hurricane Rafael aid can be narrowed, starting with how agencies reach people who can't come to them.
body: Dr. Sofia Marquez has spent years studying who gets help after disasters. A day after releasing her analysis of Hurricane Rafael aid, she wanted to talk about what comes next.
"I don't want this number framed and hung on a wall," said Marquez, a disaster equity researcher at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi. "I want it to change how the next dollar moves."

The analysis, by Marquez and Coastline Public Radio, found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.
Marquez laid out five recommendations drawn from her research.

Go door to door. "If the people who need help most can't get to a recovery center, the recovery center has to get to them," she said. Registration teams in the hardest-hit neighborhoods, with paper and phone options for people without internet, would reach households that online systems miss.

Follow the bus lines. Recovery centers and pop-up registration sites should sit on bus routes and near the churches and neighborhood hubs residents already trust. After the storm, those hubs handed out food and water before official distribution reached some streets.

Make help human and multilingual. "A form in English on a website is not access," Marquez said. She said trained neighbors, church volunteers and community health workers who speak the neighborhood's languages are often trusted more than a stranger with a clipboard.

Plan before the next storm. Before Rafael, county emergency managers urged residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance, and advocates pushed for more evacuation rides. Marquez said those lists could do double duty after a storm, showing responders which households may need a knock rather than a link.

Measure as you go. "We did this analysis three months after landfall," she said. "Agencies can track who's applying and who's getting paid, by neighborhood, every week. Then you fix the gap in December instead of reading about it in March."
Marquez said none of the recommendations require new technology. "It's shoe leather," she said. "It's the oldest tool we have."
Registration for FEMA individual assistance opened Nov. 13 and remains open.

stories.headline: County, FEMA to send aid registration teams door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods
stories.dek: The announcement comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received storm aid at about half their share of residents.
body: County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that aid registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone, bringing federal disaster aid applications to residents who have not been able to get to them.

"If you can't get to us, we'll come to you," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We're going to knock on doors, and we're going to keep knocking."

The announcement came two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found that low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents, and that their median 911 response time was 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, said residents should know how to recognize the teams. "Our people carry federal photo ID, and they will never ask you for money," Ostrander said. "If someone at your door asks for a fee, or for your account password, that's not us. Close the door and call the helpline."
FEMA added extra verification to applicant accounts after saying Nov. 24 that 410 accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, who rents near the bay and does not own a car, applied the week registration opened Nov. 13 after riding two buses to a recovery center. Her application is still pending. She said the teams should start with her neighbors.
"There's a lady on my street who's 80 and doesn't have a phone. Knock on her door first," Elizondo said. "Then come to mine, and I'll make coffee."
Officials did not release a schedule Wednesday. FEMA individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers.

stories.headline: Aid teams knocking? How to tell a real registration team from a scam
stories.dek: The county and FEMA say registration teams will go door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's how to make sure the person at your door is legitimate.
body: Aid registration is coming to your front door. Here's how to make sure the person knocking is the real thing.

County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone. The move comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

"Every one of our people will have federal photo ID, and none of them will charge you a fee," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "If you're not sure, ask to see the badge, and call the helpline to check."
How to spot a real team:
They show federal photo identification.
They never ask for money. Applying for FEMA aid is free.
They never ask for your bank PIN or your account passwords.
They don't pressure you to sign anything on the spot.
Red flags:
Someone asks for a fee to "speed up" your application.

Someone asks for your FEMA account password. FEMA said last month that 410 applicant accounts were taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites, and it added extra verification after that.
Someone sends you a link by text instead of pointing you to the official FEMA website or app.
If something feels wrong, close the door and call the FEMA helpline or local police.
Already applied? You don't need to apply again; your status and deposit details are on FEMA's official website or app.
Haven't applied? Registration remains open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

stories.headline: Door-to-door aid registration is coming. Researchers and neighbors say it's a start.
stories.dek: County and FEMA officials will send registration teams into low-income surge-zone neighborhoods, two days after Coastline's analysis found those neighborhoods got about half their share of aid.
body: On Monday, an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and Dr. Sofia Marquez of Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi found that low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. On Tuesday, Marquez said the first fix should be going door to door. On Wednesday, county and FEMA officials announced teams would do exactly that.

Marquez was careful not to claim credit. "Lots of people have been saying this for months, starting with the neighbors themselves," she said. "It's the right first step. The test is whether it reaches the people who aren't on anybody's list. The renter in the back unit. The grandmother without a phone. If the teams find them, the number moves."

The door-to-door registration will focus on low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, the same areas where residents reported waiting days for help after the storm and where many households don't have a car.
Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm, said she was ready to help the teams find people.
"My door's open, and my list is long," Whitfield said. "I know who's sick, who's alone, who's scared of anybody with a clipboard. Let me walk with them the first day, and people will open up."

Marquez said she hopes the effort is measured, not just announced. "Count the doors, count the applications, count the dollars, by neighborhood," she said. "Then show us. If it works, we'll know. If it doesn't, we'll know that too."

For neighbors wary of strangers at the door, FEMA says its staff carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Federal individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 and remains open online, by phone and at recovery centers for anyone who has not yet applied.

Marquez said the 911 findings deserve their own response. The median 911 response time in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods was 2.1 times that of high-income areas. "Door-to-door helps with aid," she said. "It doesn't answer why help took more than twice as long to arrive in the first place. That's a conversation for before the next storm."
